decisions.reason: The proposed analysis and Ground Truth G02 share the main scientific objective of detecting swapped or misassigned spots in tissue sections. Both analyses focus on using spatial gene expression and anatomical context to identify spots that are inconsistent with their expected neighboring tissue profiles. The proposed analysis refines detection of misassigned spots using expression and spatial geometry, similar to G02's approach of identifying locations inconsistent with neighboring anatomy in a brain section.

The proposed analysis focuses on correcting artifacts through local neighborhood imputation by estimating and replacing suspect expression profiles leveraging spatial context. The main scientific objective is to correct the artifacts themselves rather than evaluate the effectiveness of correction using any specific tissue type or measuring specific improvement metrics post-correction (e.g., species assignment, marker specificity). None of the ground-truth analyses focus on the core objective of artifact correction per se; instead, they measure outcomes in specific biological systems, like human-mouse chimeras, brain layers, pancreatic tumors, or colorectal tissues, after artifact corrections. Therefore, the proposed analysis does not match any of the ground-truth analyses, as they focus on evaluating changes in biological marker conditions or spatial mapping post-correction, rather than the process or methodology of correction itself.

The proposed analysis aims to assess marker gene specificity before and after quality control, which aligns with the objective of determining improved marker specificity post-correction. Ground-truth analysis G02, which involves improving marker specificity in brain layers by comparing marker-gene maps before and after correction to quantify improved specificity, matches the main scientific objective of the proposal.

The proposed analysis focuses on detecting and correcting cross-contamination in mixed-species scenarios using species-specific transcriptomic signatures. This aligns with ground-truth analysis G06, which also involves using species-specific transcripts in a mixed-species context (human-mouse chimera) to validate corrections. In both analyses, the main objective is to ensure species identity and correct assignments based on species-specific profiles.

The proposed analysis focuses on assessing spatial boundary integrity by analyzing expression gradients and distinguishing between true anatomical discontinuities and artifact-induced changes. In contrast, the ground-truth analyses primarily focus on correcting spatial omics data to improve marker specificity, spatial clustering, or assigning tissue identity, particularly in response to contamination or swaps. While both involve evaluating and possibly correcting spatial data, the proposed analysis's main scientific objective of analyzing boundary integrity does not directly align with any specific aim in the ground-truth set, which is focused more on improving data quality in specific contexts (e.g., tumor boundaries, brain layers) rather than evaluating boundary integrity itself.

The proposed analysis focuses on quantifying and correcting contamination in spatial transcriptomics data through simulation. It emphasizes understanding contamination influences and improving correction strategies. This aligns with G06 'Evaluate robustness to swap burden,' which also deals with varying contamination (swap burden) and evaluating correction efficacy vis-à-vis marker specificity and domains.

The proposed analysis focuses on using deconvolution to address and repair spots with mixed RNA signals, particularly focusing on improving the accuracy of gene expression matrices by anchoring corrections in a spatial context. This aligns with Ground Truth G01, which is concerned with correcting contamination or mixed signals in spatial-omics data by evaluating the restoration of marker specificity and spatial domains. Both analyses share the main scientific objective of disentangling and correcting mixed or contaminated signals in spatial-omics data to enhance the accuracy of the signal interpretation.

The proposed analysis focuses on the downstream impact of spatial quality control, specifically on clustering and cell-type annotation. While the exact specifics are not identical, this aligns with the main scientific objective of G06, which also investigates the effect of correction (specifically removal of swapped spots) on clustering and tissue-domain specificity. Both analyses focus on assessing the influence of quality corrections on downstream spatial clustering outcomes in relevant biological contexts.
